sections.b: Jeremiah 31:31–34 is the only Old Testament passage that says "new covenant." The LORD says he will cut it with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, "not like" the covenant of the Exodus, which they broke. He will put his law inside them and write it on their hearts, he will be their God and they his people, all will know him, and he will forgive their guilt and no longer remember their sin. Its newness is in what the LORD does inside people, not in a different law. The verses are quoted in full in Hebrews 8:8–12, and in part in Hebrews 10:16–17, and Jesus names his cup "the new covenant" in Luke 22:20 and 1 Corinthians 11:25 (Matthew and Mark have "the covenant," echoing Exodus 24:8). Radak, the medieval Jewish commentator, held that the Torah stays and that the new thing is that Israel will keep it. Christians differ on whether the covenant is made with the church, with Israel, or with the one people of God (see the cards on the church-israel page). The Qumran community called itself the "new covenant" (CD VI, 19). Jeremiah 31:35–37 grounds the promise in the fixed order of creation, as Jeremiah 33:20–26 does with the covenant of day and night.
sections.refs: Jeremiah 31:31–34; Jeremiah 31:35–37; Jeremiah 32:40; Ezekiel 36:26–27; Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25; 2 Corinthians 3:6; Hebrews 8:8–13; Hebrews 10:16–17

common: Jeremiah 31:31–34 is the center of the Old Testament's promise of a new covenant, and the New Testament sees it fulfilled in Jesus.
uncommon: Some scholars read the passage as promising a renewed, not a replaced, covenant (Radak's Jewish reading and Messianic Jewish readings).

sections.h: Hananiah and the test of a prophet (Jeremiah 28)
sections.b: In 594/593 BC the prophet Hananiah told the Temple crowd, in the LORD's name, that Babylon's yoke was already broken and the exiles would be home in two years. Jeremiah answered "Amen," then said that a prophet of peace is known only when his word comes true, and later that Hananiah had made the people trust a lie (Jeremiah 28:15). Hananiah died two months later (28:17). The chapter combines the two tests of Deuteronomy: fulfillment (Deuteronomy 18:21–22) and faithfulness to the LORD (Deuteronomy 13:1–5), and the rule that a prophet who speaks what the LORD did not tell him must die (Deuteronomy 18:20). The book's key word for the false message is sheqer, "lie" (27:10, 14, 15, 16; 28:15; 29:9, 21, 23, 31). Critics note that the rule that prophets of peace need proof is not universal, since some earlier prophets also announced rescue and Jeremiah's own warnings were conditional (18:7–10).
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 13:1–5; Deuteronomy 18:20–22; Jeremiah 28:1–17; Jeremiah 29:8–9; Jeremiah 18:7–10; Jeremiah 23:9–40

common: Jeremiah 28 is the Bible's main story of a contest between two prophets and how it was decided.
uncommon: Some interpreters hold that Hananiah was sincere and mistaken rather than a deliberate liar.

sections.b: Jeremiah wrote from Jerusalem to the Judeans taken to Babylon in 597 BC with an instruction that was unwelcome: build houses, plant gardens, marry, have children, "seek the peace of the city" and pray for it, because their peace is tied to the city's peace (Jeremiah 29:5–7). The exile would last about seventy years (29:10). Cuneiform tablets from the Judean village of Al-Yahudu, written in Babylonia from about 572 BC, show exiles farming and keeping records, as the letter implies. The letter began a tradition of Jewish and Christian thinking about how to live as a minority in a foreign land; Augustine used it for Christians in the earthly city (City of God 19.26). The promise that follows, a future and a hope (29:11), was addressed to the whole community.

common: The letter in Jeremiah 29 tells exiles to settle and pray for Babylon.
uncommon: Some scholars think the letter has been expanded after the exile, since the Greek lacks several verses.

sections.b: In the letter to the exiles Jeremiah says, "When seventy years for Babylon are over, I will turn my attention to you" (Jeremiah 29:10; compare 25:11–12). The number can be counted from 605 BC (Nebuchadnezzar's rise) to 538 (Cyrus's decree, about 67 years), or from 586 (the Temple's fall) to 516 (its rebuilding, exactly 70). Many scholars take it as a round number for a lifetime, as in Psalm 90:10. The Greek reads "when seventy years are about to be completed for Babylon." 2 Chronicles 36:21 ties the number to the land's Sabbaths, and Daniel 9:2, 24 reinterprets it as seventy weeks of years.
sections.refs: Jeremiah 25:11–12; Jeremiah 29:10; 2 Chronicles 36:21; Zechariah 1:12; Daniel 9:2; Daniel 9:24

sections.b: In his Temple sermon Jeremiah says the LORD will make this house "like Shiloh" (Jeremiah 26:6; compare 7:12–14). The priests and prophets demand his death; the officials and elders acquit him, citing Micah's warning under Hezekiah (26:18; Micah 3:12). Shiloh's shrine fell after the ark was lost to the Philistines (1 Samuel 4) and was remembered as a place the LORD abandoned (Psalm 78:60). Excavators have reported a destruction layer there from about 1050 BC (Danish excavations of 1926-63; Israel Finkelstein's from 1981), though the site was lived in thinly later. Jeremiah's point was that a holy place is no guarantee of safety.
sections.refs: 1 Samuel 4:1–11; Psalm 78:60; Jeremiah 7:12–14; Jeremiah 26:6; Jeremiah 26:9; Jeremiah 26:18

sections.h: The Temple trial and the vessels (Jeremiah 26–28)
sections.b: Jeremiah 26 shows a prophet put on trial for saying the Temple could be destroyed. Jeremiah 27–28 turn to the Temple's bronze vessels: the pillars, the Sea, the stands and the smaller objects. Some were taken in 597 BC, the rest in 586, and Hananiah said they would be back in two years. Jeremiah answered that they would return only when the LORD called for them (27:22). Cyrus returned 5,400 vessels under Sheshbazzar (Ezra 1:7–11). Jesus' trial includes a charge about the Temple (Matthew 26:61).
sections.refs: Jeremiah 26:1–24; Jeremiah 27:16–22; Jeremiah 28:3; 2 Kings 24:13; 2 Kings 25:13–17; Ezra 1:7–11; Matthew 26:61

sections.b: In 594/593 BC Jeremiah wore a yoke and told the envoys visiting Jerusalem (possibly to plan a revolt) of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre and Sidon, and King Zedekiah, that the LORD had given all these lands to "Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, my servant" (Jeremiah 27:6). The title does not mean that Nebuchadnezzar believed in the LORD; it means the LORD used him (25:9; 43:10; compare Cyrus, Isaiah 45:1). Nations that served him would stay in their land; those that rebelled would be destroyed. The same God would also bring Babylon down when its time came (27:7; 25:12).

In the Book of Consolation the LORD says that after he breaks the yoke of the strangers, his people "will serve the LORD their God and David their king, whom I will raise up for them" (Jeremiah 30:9). The ruler of 30:21 comes "from his own people" and approaches the LORD. The same hope is stated in Jeremiah 23:5–6 and 33:15–17 (the Branch), Hosea 3:5 and Ezekiel 34:23–24; 37:24–25. The Aramaic Targum of the Prophets reads 30:9 as "Messiah the son of David." Christian readers see Jesus (Luke 1:32–33).
sections.refs: Jeremiah 30:9; Jeremiah 30:21; Jeremiah 23:5–6; Jeremiah 33:15–17; Hosea 3:5; Ezekiel 34:23–24; 2 Samuel 7:12–16; Luke 1:32–33

sections.h: The ruler from Jacob's own people (Jeremiah 30:8–9, 21)
sections.b: Jeremiah 30:9 ("David their king") and 30:21 (a leader "from his own people") are treated under the topic Davidic covenant, with the Targum's reading of 30:9 and the Christian and Jewish readings. They join Jeremiah 23:5–6 and 33:15–17 in the Old Testament's picture of a coming king from David's house.

Jeremiah 31:15–17 pictures Rachel, mother of Joseph's sons (so of Ephraim and Manasseh) and of Benjamin, weeping for her exiled children at Ramah, a town in Benjamin where the Babylonians gathered captives (40:1). The LORD tells her to stop weeping: her children will come home. Matthew 2:17–18 quotes the verse for the grief at Bethlehem when Herod killed the infants. Rachel's tomb was placed near Bethlehem in Genesis 35:16–20 and in Benjamin in 1 Samuel 10:2. Readers differ on whether Matthew sees a prediction or a pattern.

sections.h: "I will change my mind" in Jeremiah 26
sections.b: The LORD says in Jeremiah 26:3 that if the people turn back he will change his mind about the harm he has planned, and the elders remember that this is what happened under Hezekiah (26:19). The Hebrew verb nicham is the same as in Jonah 3:10 and Exodus 32:14. Jeremiah 18:7–10 states the principle: a threat or a promise can be reversed when the people respond. Chapter 26 shows that this principle is what makes Jeremiah's warnings a call, not only a prediction.
sections.refs: Jeremiah 18:7–10; Jeremiah 26:3; Jeremiah 26:13; Jeremiah 26:19; Jonah 3:10; Exodus 32:14

sections.b: Jeremiah 31:29–30 says that in days to come people will no longer say, "The fathers ate sour grapes, and the children's teeth go numb"; each one will die for his own guilt. Ezekiel 18:2–4 quotes the same proverb and teaches individual responsibility, and Deuteronomy 24:16 lays down that children are not put to death for parents. Yet Exodus 20:5 and Jeremiah 32:18 speak of the guilt of the fathers falling on the children. Readers reconcile the two by distinguishing family consequences in this life from accountability before God.

The last promise of the new covenant is forgiveness: the LORD forgives their guilt and will remember their sin no more (Jeremiah 31:34). In the Bible, God's "remembering" is acting on something, so not remembering means not holding it against someone (compare Isaiah 43:25; Psalm 103:12; Micah 7:19). Hebrews 8:12 and 10:17 quote the line to say that Christ's sacrifice makes further offerings for sin unnecessary.
sections.refs: Jeremiah 31:34; Isaiah 43:25; Psalm 103:12; Micah 7:19; Hebrews 8:12; Hebrews 10:17

sections.h: Jeremiah 31:31–37: the covenant and Israel's permanence
sections.b: Jeremiah 31 is at the center of debate over the church and Israel. The new covenant is made "with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah" (31:31), and 31:35–37 says Israel will cease to be a nation only if the sun, moon and the foundations of the earth fail. Christians who hold that God still has a plan for the Jewish people point to these verses with Romans 11:1–2, 29. Others read "Israel" as the people of God, including Gentile believers (Galatians 6:16; Hebrews 8). Jewish readers see a promise of the permanence of the Jewish people. See the cards on this page.
sections.refs: Jeremiah 31:31; Jeremiah 31:35–37; Romans 11:1–2; Romans 11:29; Galatians 6:16; Hebrews 8:8

sections.h: The prophet on trial and in dispute (Jeremiah 26–29)
sections.b: Chapters 26–29 show Jeremiah in conflict with the priests and prophets who accused him of treason in the Temple (26), with the envoys of the five kings and their prophets (27), with Hananiah, whose death in two months settled the contest (28) and, in a letter, with the prophets Ahab, Zedekiah and Shemaiah among the exiles (29). In each case he is shown as a man sent, who waits for the word before he answers (28:12), who is protected only by a few officials such as Ahikam son of Shaphan (26:24), and who tells people the hard thing, that Babylon will rule for seventy years.

In a shout of joy, Jeremiah 31:7 tells Israel to pray, "LORD, save your people, the remnant of Israel," or, as the Greek reads, "The LORD has saved his people." The remnant here is the survivors of the sword (31:2) who will be gathered, including the blind, the lame and women in labor (31:8). It is a remnant that will return, not a remnant of the faithful chosen from a rebellious nation.

Jeremiah is told several times not to intercede for Judah (Jeremiah 7:16; 11:14; 14:11). In 27:18 he turns the matter around: if the prophets of peace really have the LORD's word, they should plead with him that the remaining Temple vessels not go to Babylon. The Torah's model intercessors are Moses and Samuel (Exodus 32:11–14; 1 Samuel 12:23; Jeremiah 15:1).
sections.refs: Jeremiah 27:18; Jeremiah 7:16; Jeremiah 11:14; Jeremiah 14:11; Jeremiah 15:1; Exodus 32:11–14
